Spatial across ages: 4–5 years · 5–7 years · 7–9 years · 9–12 years · 12–25 years

Between ages 4 and 5, children make significant strides in understanding and using spatial terms to describe relationships. They typically begin to grasp basic prepositions like above, below, in front of, behind, and between, applying them not just egocentrically (relative to themselves) but also to describe object-to-object relations in a scene 1. For example, a 5-year-old can follow instructions such as "put the toy between the boxes" or "stand behind me," whereas a 3- or 4-year-old might still confuse these terms. By this age children also begin to grasp left vs. right on their own bodies (e.g. identifying their left hand) and use these terms in context, though consistently applying left/right remains challenging; true mastery of left/right generally comes between 5 and 7 years 1. Improvements in spatial vocabulary are directly tied to improvements in spatial problem solving (e.g block design tests) 2.

At 4-5 years old, children show rapid gains in their ability to mentally manipulate spatial information, although these skills are still developing and error-prone. One key milestone is the emergence of mental rotation ability (the capacity to imagine objects turning in space and recognize how they would look from different angles). Classic experiments have demonstrated that by around 5 years of age children start to perform above chance on simplified mental rotation tasks. For instance, when shown a shape and asked to pick which of two holes it would fit into (with the shape presented at various rotated angles), 5-year-olds’ error rates and reaction times increase systematically with the degree of rotation, much like adults who take longer for larger mental rotations 3, 4. This linear increase in difficulty with angle suggests that the 5-year-old is indeed mentally rotating the figure to align it, rather than randomly guessing. In contrast, 4-year-olds often perform at chance on such tasks, not yet showing a reliable increase in response time with angle and frequently resorting to guessing 3. Another data point lies in the mental rotation study mentioned earlier; in this task (where pairs of asymmetrical ghost figures and a hole are presented; the child must determine which ghost fits in the hole by mentally rotating it), 10% of 3-year-olds and 40% of 4-year-olds perform above chance, while 95% of 5-year-olds do 5.

In tandem with object rotation skills, spatial perspective-taking (the ability to imagine how the world looks from another viewpoint) improves notably by age 4-5. At earlier ages, children are notoriously egocentric in the spatial sense: they tend to assume others see what they see. By 4, however, children show the first signs of overcoming this egocentrism. Researchers distinguish Level 1 perspective-taking (understanding what another person can or cannot see) and Level 2 perspective-taking (understanding how another person sees something, i.e. the appearance from their angle) 6. Level 1 develops in infancy and toddlerhood (see the 12-24 months section). Level 2 perspective-taking first appears around 4-5 years of age 6, but remains nascent. They can understand that a person sitting opposite them sees a picture "upside down" relative to their own view, or that a toy hidden behind a screen is visible to them but not to someone on the other side; conversely, when a 4- to 5-year old is shown a tabletop display and asked to choose a photograph that depicts what a doll would see from a different position, their performance is typically at chance level, frequently defaulting to their own viewpoint 6. The ability to mentally rotate scenes (especially those with mutiple objects) continues to develop across the ensuing years, suggesting that 4- to 5-year-olds are still laying the groundwork for mental rotation (by learning to recognize basic spatial relationships and expanding their knowledge of objects/places). Perspective-taking tasks ask what another viewer sees. (Figure). Perspective-taking difficulty depends on scene complexity. (Figure).

At this stage, children become better at forming mental representations of and navigating their environment, allowing more flexible travel beyond simple habit or trial-and-error; their navigation is, however, still not nearly as efficient or flexible as that of older children and adults. One major development is the child’s increasing use of landmarks to orient and navigate; younger children (toddlers) navigate mostly egocentrically (e.g they might remember a route as a series of body turns (go left, then right) or actions ("pass the sofa then the door")), while four- and five-year-olds begin to encode the environment in relation to external cues (allocentrically; e.g "the playground is next to the big red house"). After disorientation, both 4- and 5-year-olds can reliably reorient by extended surface geometry (e.g if the room is rectangular/irregular) 7, but five-year-olds are more likely to recruit landmarks in the kinds of "large-room" or ecologically valid settings where four-year-olds often fail unless scaffolded by language 8, 9 (although 3- and 4-year-olds have been shown to reliably use landmarks in straightforward scenarios where they remain oriented towards the goal 10). In everyday terms, a 5-year-old might start saying, "We turn at the big oak tree to go home" (using that landmark in conjunction with a sense of left/right) whereas a 3-year-old might only retrace the route without explicitly referencing the tree. The progression is from landmark-as-beacon (toddler will go straight to an object in view) to using landmark configurations and spatial layouts (older child can keep track of where things are even when not in view, by remembering how landmarks are arranged around them). Another emerging navigational skill at this age is path integration (the ability to update one’s position by tracking self-movement (the distances and turns traveled) even without obvious external cues); in one study, blindfolded 5-year-olds who were led along a path with a couple of turns could successfully orient back to the start point on their own on the majority of trials, though often not as precisely as adults 11. Moreover, some children at this age can go beyond simple homing and begin to form a rudimentary cognitive map of the space using path integration; in the same study, a substantial subset of 5-year-olds could even use their path integration-derived knowledge to take novel shortcuts between locations (mapping rather than just retracing routes) 11. A developmental experiment tests landmarks during navigation (Figure) 13. The study compares landmark and rotation conditions (Figure).

Five-year-olds also begin to grasp symbolic spatial representations like maps and models. The famous "scale model" experiments by DeLoache showed that 2½-year-olds struggle to relate a model room to a larger room, but by 3 years they start to understand it when helped, and by 4-5 years most children can use a small model or a simple map to find an object in a real space. By age 5, many children find it exciting to follow a basic treasure map or use a picture diagram to locate something, demonstrating that they can translate between abstract spatial representations and real-world locations 12.

Overall, the 4-5 age range is a period of rapid improvement in navigational cognition. Children move from an almost purely egocentric and trial-and-error approach toward using external references and internal cues in concert. They do, however, still rely on salient structures (like room shape or a prominent landmark) to reorient when disoriented, highlighting a continuing bias for geometric framework at this age (which can be framed as prefrontal/premotor networks not yet discovering better strategies).
